questions.key_step: Perfect square (|c|-1)^2=0 from |c-a|=2sqrt2 and a.c=|c|.
questions.justification: Routine chain: cross product magnitude, expand |c-a|^2, spot a perfect square, then use |u x v|=|u||v|sin. No real insight beyond spotting the square; options allow a check. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2, magnitude conditions then area).

questions.key_step: Projection = |BA|cos(angle B) with the cosine rule.
questions.justification: Single familiar move (projection as |BA|cos B, then cosine rule) applied once; no decision. Close to the direct-formula anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), nudged to 1 for the extra cosine-rule step.

questions.key_step: Write a = lambda b + mu c; a.d=0 and |a|^2=10 give a = ±(3j-k); [a b c]=0.
questions.justification: Two linked ideas (coplanarity as linear combination, then triple-product evaluation) with several routine computations; 'possible value' means the sign must be tracked. Same chain-of-routine-steps profile as 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Cross-product relations force a, b, c mutually perpendicular with |b|=1, |c|=2.
questions.justification: Four statements to verify after one structural deduction (orthogonality and magnitudes); each check is routine, 'not true' phrasing adds care. Similar to 2021-P2-Q5 (L2, projections and areas from cross product) but with a single-correct format.

questions.key_step: Coplanar => det = 0, reduce using R3-R2 and column operations.
questions.justification: One familiar move (coplanarity as a zero determinant) followed by routine row/column reduction; options make the check easy. Same family as 2023-P2-Q4 (L1, coplanarity check).

questions.key_step: Zero determinant gives c^2 = ab.
questions.justification: One familiar move (coplanar -> determinant) and a three-term expansion; options available. Same level as 2023-P2-Q4 (L1).

questions.key_step: sin theta = 4/5 from the cross-product magnitude, then |cos theta| = 3/5.
questions.justification: Two standard formulae applied directly with a Pythagorean triple; essentially no decision. Sits next to the direct-formula anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), kept at 1 because two formulas must be combined.

questions.key_step: (a-b)xb = axb, then repeated BAC-CAB with a.b=7, |a|^2=6, |b|^2=14.
questions.justification: Long nested expression but each step is a standard identity; options let the student check at the end. Routine chain, no insight beyond noticing the first simplification; comparable to 2025-P1-Q16 (L2, cross-product relations).

questions.key_step: BAC-CAB then |a|=|b||b x c|, or dot with a and c to get cos^2 theta = 1/2.
questions.justification: A single numerical equation after a standard expansion; the unknown angle comes out from a short chain of dot products. Slightly longer than a one-trick item, no unfamiliar idea. Nearest 2025-P1-Q16 (L2).

questions.key_step: Apply the shortest-distance formula and solve |2alpha+15|=27.
questions.justification: Direct application of a standard formula once; the numerical format and the sign choice (alpha>0) add only a trivial step. Near 2024-P1-Q16 (L0, direct coplanar-lines computation), kept at 1 for the cross-product and modulus.

questions.key_step: |a+b+c|=r sqrt3 so cos theta=1/sqrt3, then double angle.
questions.justification: One familiar move (equal inclination with orthogonal triad gives cos theta = 1/sqrt3) followed by a double-angle formula. Same direct-formula family as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), kept at 1 for the two stages.

questions.key_step: Equal magnitudes fix p=2; tan theta = cross/dot of the plane vectors.
questions.justification: Two routine stages (solve for p, then compute tan of the angle between two vectors) in numerical format with surd arithmetic; no unfamiliar idea. Similar demand to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Two dot-product equations leave r = alpha(i-j+k); magnitude fixes |alpha|.
questions.justification: Two linear perpendicularity equations and a magnitude: one standard idea, applied directly, numerical answer but tiny search space. Close to 2024-P1-Q12 (L1, dot/cross condition fixes parameters).

questions.key_step: Expand the two dot products and solve the two homogeneous equations for |a|=|b|, a.b=|b|^2/2.
questions.justification: Routine expansion and elimination with exact arithmetic in numerical format, no new idea. Same chain-of-routine-steps profile as 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Dot a x b = c with c: [a,b,c]=|c|^2=2, then projection formula.
questions.justification: One neat move (triple product from a x b = c) plus routine projection length and a cross product; numerical but short, no casework. More steps than 2024-P2-Q11 (L0, dot with p x q) and far lighter than 2026-P2-Q1 (L3).

questions.key_step: a.b and b.c give alpha*beta=2, 2alpha+beta=-5; integer root; then 3x3 determinant.
questions.justification: Routine chain: two dot products, a quadratic with an integrality filter, then a determinant. Numerical format but no insight or casework, so L2 (three or more routine steps). Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) minus its trigonometric/geometric step.

questions.key_step: Rewrite to symmetric form, then coplanarity determinant gives (b-1)/(ab)=0.
questions.justification: Standard coplanarity determinant with the extra care of converting the non-standard form x=ay-1=z-2 and simplifying a messy determinant; options help. Close to 2023-P2-Q4 (L3, coplanarity check) but only one condition, so L2.

questions.key_step: Foot of perpendicular -> midpoint -> image Q; plane normal = direction of L.
questions.justification: Standard chain (foot, image, plane) with careful arithmetic; options allow a check. Nearest in demand to 2024-P1-Q16 (L3, direct computations) but all steps are textbook, so L2.

questions.key_step: Direction n1 x n2, parametrise L, impose PN . direction = 0.
questions.justification: Three routine stages (direction, point on L, foot) with fractional arithmetic; option-based so checkable. Level equals other direct 3D computation anchors like 2024-P1-Q16 (L3) but lighter, so L2.

questions.key_step: Reduce to symmetric form, p x q, then SD formula with unknown lambda.
questions.justification: Single textbook formula applied after converting the lines to symmetric form, followed by a modulus equation; options allow checking. Three routine steps with no insight: L2 (2024-P1-Q16 L3 is direct but with more stages).

questions.key_step: Q from PQ parallel to plane (PQ . n = 0); then the 90-alpha trick or right triangle.
questions.justification: Locate Q by the parallel-to-plane condition then use the right triangle PNQ; three routine steps, options available, no insight beyond the right-angle observation. Level 2 as a short multi-step chain.

questions.key_step: Normal = n1 x n2, then plane through the point.
questions.justification: One familiar move (cross product of normals) followed by a plane through a point and a sum; options present. Like 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) in being direct but with a short chain, so L1.

questions.key_step: Equate general points, y and z equations fix t1=1, t2=-1, then plane gives alpha and beta.
questions.justification: Routine intersection of two lines with parameters followed by a plane substitution and bookkeeping of alpha, beta; no insight but several steps and a sign trap in beta. L2 (comparable to 2023-P2-Q4 L3 but straighter).

questions.key_step: Vector in plane and perpendicular to r: lambda (p x q) x r, then scalar condition.
questions.justification: Needs the (p x q) x r idea (or a linear system) after finding the plane direction vectors; a few standard steps and numerical answer. L2 (routine chain, no real insight; 2026-P2-Q1 is L3 for a longer geometric chain).

questions.key_step: Coplanarity determinant is linear in k.
questions.justification: Direct application of the coplanarity determinant with one unknown: one familiar move applied once. Level 1 (JEE Main), numerical but no steps beyond a 3x3 determinant.

questions.key_step: Normal = AB x p = 14(1,1,1); plane x+y+z=3; distance from origin.
questions.justification: Routine chain: coplanarity determinant for the plane, then point-plane distance; numerical but arithmetic is small and checkable by substituting A and B. L2.

questions.key_step: General point of line QR in the plane equation.
questions.justification: One familiar move (line-plane intersection) followed by a distance: direct, no decisions, only one parameter. L1.

questions.key_step: Cyclic triple product or a x (a x c) expansion.
questions.justification: Two-stage vector-triple-product manipulation; a student who sees the cyclic property finishes in two lines but the standard route needs the expansion and dot trick. L2; option-based. Slightly above 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) for the identity needed.

questions.key_step: Squaring the magnitude condition gives a quadratic in |b| using a.b=|a||b|cos60.
questions.justification: Single familiar move (expand dot products, solve one quadratic); a prepared student does it in under two minutes with options to check against.

questions.key_step: BAC-CAB expansion of each triple product, then expressing r in the perpendicular triad.
questions.justification: Chain of three vector-triple-product expansions with an unknown vector in a triad; each step routine but needs care with signs and the 'a.b=0' simplification.

questions.key_step: Projection formula p.q/|q| with q = sum of the two vectors; squaring cancels the lambda^2 terms.
questions.justification: One standard formula applied once, followed by a short algebraic solve; numerical format but no trap.

questions.key_step: Lagrange identity for |bxc|^2 gives beta = -2, -4; each beta fixes alpha via a.b=0.
questions.justification: Two conditions chained with two branches to compare; numerical format means no options, but each step is a standard identity.

questions.key_step: Recognise v is parallel to c x (a x b) (plane of a,b and perpendicular to c), then fix the scalar from the projection.
questions.justification: Three-stage chain (triple product, scalar from projection, norm) with exact arithmetic and no options to check against; idea is standard but needs care.

questions.key_step: Family of planes pi1 + lambda pi2 with normal perpendicular to the given plane's normal.
questions.justification: Routine two-step planes chain with options to test; no insight needed, but several standard results are chained.

questions.key_step: Family of planes through the intersection line, lambda fixed by the given point.
questions.justification: Single standard move (pencil of planes) followed by substitution of options.

questions.key_step: Pencil of planes P1 + lambda P2, then distance-from-origin condition gives a quadratic in lambda.
questions.justification: Routine chain: family of planes, distance formula, solve the quadratic, simplify; options available as a check. Slightly more algebra than the one-move planes questions.

questions.key_step: Parametrise the line through the point along the given direction and find where it meets the plane.
questions.justification: One familiar move (point along a direction meets a plane), a short substitution.

questions.key_step: Choose lambda in pi1 + lambda pi2 so the x-coefficient vanishes (parallel to x-axis).
questions.justification: Single family-of-planes move with an easy normality condition; options are simple to match.

questions.key_step: Eliminate n to get 2l^2+5lm+2m^2=0, giving two direction-ratio sets and their dot product.
questions.justification: Elimination, factorisation and two direction-ratio sets: routine multi-step, options available.

questions.key_step: Pencil of planes with lambda from the given point; then normalise the constant to 3 (sign flip).
questions.justification: One familiar move plus a normalisation step where a sign slip is possible; options available.

questions.key_step: Direction of the line = n1 x n2, line through the origin, foot of the perpendicular via PR.b = 0.
questions.justification: Several routine steps (cross product, parametrise, foot of perpendicular, length); options available to check.

questions.key_step: Direction of the line from the two normals, then a foot of the perpendicular (here already at the chosen point).
questions.justification: Routine chain: direction by cross product, point on line, foot of perpendicular, length; options available.

questions.key_step: Choose the sign of the bisector formula using the sign of a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2, then test the options.
questions.justification: One standard formula plus one sign decision (acute vs obtuse), then a substitution check on four options; options let the student verify. Chain is short and routine, similar in demand to 2021-P1-Q8 (L2, direct plane computation).

questions.key_step: A line lies in a plane iff its direction is perpendicular to the normal and one point of it satisfies the plane.
questions.justification: Two standard conditions, each a one-line substitution; no insight and no long chain. Easier than 2021-P1-Q8 (L2, multi-step plane computation), a Main-level one-move application.

questions.key_step: Put the parametric point of the line into the plane to get one parameter, then use the distance formula.
questions.justification: Single familiar move (line-plane intersection by substitution) followed by a distance computation; no decisions. Level 1 as a pure Main-style routine.

questions.key_step: Reflect Q in the plane (foot of perpendicular, then midpoint) and then compute SR^2.
questions.justification: Standard mirror-image routine plus a point on the plane found from a parameter; numerical format with no options to check, several arithmetic stages. Routine chain with no new idea, so L2 (a shortcut RS = RQ exists but is optional).

questions.key_step: Projection of a line = line of intersection of the plane with the plane through the line perpendicular to it; here found via two points R and Q.
questions.justification: Four routine stages (intersection point, foot of perpendicular, line L, distance from a point to L) with exact arithmetic and no options; each stage standard but a slip ruins the answer. Nearest in spirit to 2023-P1-Q16 (L3) and above 2021-P1-Q8 (L2).

questions.key_step: The two lines are coplanar, so the plane has normal \vec d_1\times\vec d_2; the squared distance of P from it is the answer.
questions.justification: Plane through two lines by a determinant, then point-plane distance; straightforward two-stage computation with no hidden idea. Routine chain of standard results, L2.

questions.key_step: c is perpendicular to c x a, so |b|=1 becomes |c|^2(1+4 sin^2 15 deg)=1.
questions.justification: Two linked ideas: the hidden orthogonality c.(c x a)=0 and the half-angle evaluation of sin^2(15 deg) to reach a surd; options help but the algebra with surds is error prone. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3, norms of sums and differences with cross products).

questions.key_step: ( a+ b) perp ( a x  b) gives 2+2costheta+4sin^2theta=4, then both statements are direct checks.
questions.justification: Hidden orthogonality gives a quadratic in cos(theta), then two one-line checks; routine chain with options and short statements. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) but lighter since each statement is a single substitution, so L2.

questions.key_step: Find  a=5( i+ j+ k) from the projection, then  b perp  a in the plane of  a and  i with | b|=| a|.
questions.justification: Four stages: direction cosines and scaling from a projection, representing a coplanar vector, using perpendicularity and equal length, then a final projection. Each is standard but the chain with sign choices needs care. Close to 2024-P1-Q12 (L4, parameters fixed by vector conditions) but with more routine steps, so L3.

questions.key_step: Expand each triple product by BAC-CAB and note the three results are linearly dependent, so the scalar triple product is 0.
questions.justification: Three routine BAC-CAB expansions then a determinant-like expansion; no insight needed but several steps, with a cleaner insight (Jacobi identity) available. Routine chain, L2, similar to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) in length but lighter.

questions.key_step: Coplanarity fixes alpha=frac53; the plane normal is  d_1 x  d_2 and the distance is a point-plane formula.
questions.justification: Coplanarity determinant, cross product for the normal, plane equation and a distance: four routine stages, each standard, options available. L2, close to 2023-P2-Q4 (L3, coplanarity check) but without the extra checks.

questions.key_step: Write  v=x a+y b; the projection and  v. j=7 give two linear equations in x,y.
questions.justification: Setting up a coplanar vector, one projection condition and one component condition gives a 2x2 linear system, then a dot product; routine chain, options available. Comparable to 2021-P1-Q8 (L2).

questions.key_step: b x  c= a forces  a. c=0; the given vectors violate it, so no  b exists.
questions.justification: One familiar fact: a cross product is perpendicular to each factor, applied once with a one-line dot product; the 'count' framing is a trap but needs no computation. Level 1, one familiar move.

questions.key_step: Diagonals  a, b give area frac12| a x  b|; then  b perp ( a x  b) makes  c a vector in an orthogonal frame.
questions.justification: Chain of four stages: tan(theta)=1 from |a.b|=|a x b|, the area formula with diagonals, |b|, then |c| and b.c using b perpendicular to a x b; each step standard but the diagonal-area factor 1/2 is a trap. Near 2026-P2-Q1 (L3).

questions.key_step: Plane through the intersection of two planes: P1 + lambda P2 = 0 and use the given point.
questions.justification: Standard family-of-planes chain: write family, fix lambda with the point, read off normal and d, then evaluate a ratio. Every step is routine and options allow a check. Closest anchor 2026-P1-Q6 (L3) is richer (MCQ with several statements); this is plainer.

questions.key_step: Equate |a x b|^2 to 15(alpha^2+4), solve the biquadratic for alpha^2, then evaluate.
questions.justification: Cross product, a biquadratic in alpha, then a routine evaluation of |a|^2 and a.b: three or four routine steps, options present. Closest anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (L2, vector area chain).

questions.key_step: Write a = (a1,a2,a3); a x (2i+k) gives two components directly, perpendicularity gives the third.
questions.justification: Compare components of a cross product, solve a small linear system and take a projection. Routine but multi-step; options let the student check. Close to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: One component of b x c gives beta; projection formula gives alpha.
questions.justification: Two independent one-line conditions (projection formula, one cross-product component) with no chaining; options present. Level 1 as only standard moves are applied once each. Anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L0, direct vector product evaluation) is slightly simpler.

questions.key_step: Collinearity of A,B,C at alpha=1 so smallest non-collinear positive integer is 2; then median length to midpoint of BC.
questions.justification: Collinearity test with a parameter, a small trap on 'smallest positive integer', then midpoint and distance. Routine, options present; level 2. Anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

A single standard identity once the cross product is simplified; answer independent of theta. Numerical format but no casework or computation. Anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) is a single formula; this needs the identity plus a simplification, so L1.

questions.key_step: Plane through S parallel to both lines has normal d1 x d2, and since S lies on L1 and the lines meet, it passes through the origin.
questions.justification: Find the meeting point S (or use coplanarity), normal by cross product, then read a, b, d. Routine chain, numerical format, no real trap. Anchor 2024-P1-Q12 (L4) is far more involved; 2026-P1-Q6 (L3) is richer. This sits at L2.

questions.key_step: a x b is perpendicular to b, fixing lambda; then solve for a and evaluate the dot products.
questions.justification: Solve for a vector from a x b and a.b (needs a small insight that lambda is forced), then a routine evaluation. Numerical format, several stages but each routine. Anchor 2024-P1-Q12 (L4) is harder; this is a plain chain at L2.

questions.key_step: Coplanarity gives [a b c]=0 (a linear equation in c); with a.c=5 and b.c=0 solve the 3x3 system.
questions.justification: Three linear equations in c1,c2,c3 from three standard conditions, then arithmetic with 122. Numerical format, routine but fraction-heavy. Anchor 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, coplanarity with parameters) is more involved; this is plainer, L2.

questions.key_step: Normal of P2 = AB x AC, then direction of the common line = n1 x n2.
questions.justification: Two successive cross products with routine arithmetic; numerical format. Closest anchor 2026-P1-Q6 (L3) has more statements; this is a plain two-step chain, L2.

questions.key_step: Dot the given relation with c: c.(b x c)=0 kills the cross-product term, leaving c.a=0.
questions.justification: One scalar-triple-product trick (repeated vector gives zero), numerical format but no computation. Note the data are inconsistent as printed (a.b = 2, but a = -(b x c) must be perpendicular to b), so students are expected to use the trick without solving for c. Anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) is a single formula; this needs one idea, hence L1.

questions.key_step: Shortest distance = |AB.(p x q)|/|p x q| with a parameter, leading to a quadratic in lambda whose root sum is asked.
questions.justification: Standard skew-lines formula with a parameter lambda; algebra gives a quadratic and Vieta. Single standard formula plus algebra with options available; L2. Anchor 2023-P1-Q5 (L3, cube diagonals shortest distance) is richer.

questions.key_step: Equidistant points form the perpendicular bisector plane of PQ, whose normal is PQ; then angle between normals.
questions.justification: Recognise the perpendicular-bisector plane and take the angle between normals: a short, standard chain. Options present. Anchor 2024-P2-Q6 (L1, routine planes) is similar.

questions.key_step: Mirror image Q of P in the plane, then L is parallel to PQ i.e. along the normal (1,1,1); intersect L with the plane to get R.
questions.justification: Reflection formula, line parametrisation, intersection with plane, distance: four routine steps, options present. Anchor 2026-P2-Q7 (L3, foot of perpendicular and ratio point) is richer; this is routine, L2.

questions.key_step: Family P1+λP2 fixed by the point, then compare signs of the plane expression at X and Y (and combinations).
questions.justification: Routine chain: build the family plane, solve for lambda, then evaluate signs at X, Y and the combined points to reject the other options. No unfamiliar idea; option-based so answer is checkable. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2, several standard steps).

questions.key_step: Normalise 2y+3 to y+3/2 so the y-direction ratio of l2 is alpha/2; use l1 perp l2 to get alpha=3 then the angle formula.
questions.justification: Three routine stages (direction ratios, perpendicularity for alpha, angle) with one trap in the normalisation of 2y+3 and the sec^-1 form of the answer. Options help. Same demand as 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Right-angle rotation about the common line: pick lambda so the new plane's normal is perpendicular to the old one; then reflect.
questions.justification: Two routine stages (perpendicular member of the family, then image of a point) with a mildly unfamiliar 'rotation about a line' phrasing. Options allow checking. Slightly more than 2026-P2-Q1 (L2) but no new idea.

questions.key_step: Family P1+λP2 with the perpendicularity condition on normals gives λ=2 in one line.
questions.justification: One familiar move (pencil of planes with perpendicularity), a short computation and a point test. Closest in demand to 2026-P1-Q3 (L1, one standard step) with slightly more arithmetic.

questions.key_step: Eliminate m to get a quadratic in l/n and demand equal roots (D=0) for parallel lines.
questions.justification: Standard elimination in direction cosines, but the equal-roots reading of 'parallel' is the one idea students must recall; algebra is short and options confirm. Slightly above a pure routine chain; anchored at L2 like 2026-P2-Q3.

questions.key_step: Parametrise the line, impose AP perpendicular to direction, then apply the point-plane distance formula.
questions.justification: Two standard formulas used once each (foot of perpendicular, point-plane distance), nothing hidden; option-based. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0-1 direct computation); placed at L1 for the two-stage arithmetic.

questions.key_step: Direct use of the skew-lines shortest distance formula.
questions.justification: A single standard formula applied once with a cross product and a dot product; no choice or insight. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0 direct computation); at L1 for the 3x3 cross product and surd simplification.

questions.key_step: Recognise the line of intersection as t(1,1,1) through the origin, then find the two points at distance sqrt18 from P and the isosceles triangle's base and height.
questions.justification: Three routine stages (line through origin, quadratic for the two points, base-and-height area) with arithmetic care; no hidden idea. Option-based. Placed with 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Use the pencil of planes twice, one lambda per point, then compare the two normals.
questions.justification: Two applications of the same pencil-of-planes idea followed by the angle formula; routine but fairly long and arithmetic-heavy with fractional lambdas. Option-based. Matches 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Normal of the required plane is the cross product of the two given normals.
questions.justification: One standard move (cross product of normals) followed by plane through a point; short and mechanical. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0 direct computation); L1 for the extra gcd/sign bookkeeping.

questions.key_step: Image via midpoint on plane and PQ along the normal.
questions.justification: Textbook image-of-a-point computation; one standard method, single stage plus final combination. Options exist. Level matches L1 anchors such as 2026-P1-Q3 (L1).

questions.key_step: Collect powers of lambda in the plane equation to get two linear equations for p and q.
questions.justification: Two linear equations for p, q from the line-in-plane condition, then a point-plane distance and surd simplification into the option form; routine chain with one slip risk. Close to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Altitudes through H perpendicular to the given sides locate B and C.
questions.justification: Plane coordinate geometry of a triangle (not 3D) in a vector sheet; chain of line intersections, all routine. Matches 2026-P2-Q1 (L2) for routine multi-step.

questions.key_step: Image Q via the mirror formula, then plane through Q and the line via AQ x d.
questions.justification: Two standard stages (image point, plane through a point and a line) and a substitution check of four options; all familiar. Option-based so checkable. Same level as 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Parametrise A and B and set AB proportional to (1,-4,2).
questions.justification: Standard two-parameter proportionality chain with careful arithmetic; no options to check against. Similar to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2), a routine multi-step vector computation.

questions.key_step: Distance formula for skew lines with parameter a, then quadratic.
questions.justification: One standard formula applied once; the quadratic is short. Same kind of direct application as 2024-P1-Q16 (L0) but with an unknown parameter to solve for, so L1.

questions.key_step: Convert intercept form to point-direction form, then skew-line distance formula.
questions.justification: Routine chain: two intercept conversions, a cross product with surds, and the distance formula; numerical answer so no option to check. About 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: AC parallel to normal with midpoint on plane; combine with a+b+c=5.
questions.justification: Reflection set-up with three conditions and careful elimination; a slip in arithmetic changes the numerical answer. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q7 (L3) in set-up but far shorter, so L2.

questions.key_step: Foot of perpendicular by dot product, then R as midpoint of PP'.
questions.justification: Two familiar moves (foot of perpendicular, section ratio) chained with fractions; numerical so no check. Close to 2026-P2-Q7 (L3) in flavour but simpler, so L2.

questions.key_step: Foot-of-perpendicular formula applied twice, then distance.
questions.justification: A single formula used twice followed by a distance; no decision beyond recalling the formula. Near 2024-P1-Q16 (L0) / 2024-P2-Q6 (L1), so L1.

questions.key_step: Closed triangle makes (a+c)xb vanish; cosine rule for S2.
questions.justification: Two statements to check, each a short vector identity; the trap is the angle's orientation and the key's sign. Similar to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2) in demand.

questions.key_step: Lagrange's identity to get |b|^2, then projection formula.
questions.justification: One recalled identity, then a routine projection; options available to check against. Close to 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) / 2026-P2-Q1 (L2); L1.

questions.key_step: Cross product, dot with n, solve the quadratic.
questions.justification: A single routine pipeline: cross product, projection formula, quadratic; options let the student check. Level 1 by comparison with 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) and 2024-P2-Q6 (L1).

questions.key_step: Normals to the two planes, cross product for the line, supplementary angle.
questions.justification: Three routine steps (two normals, their cross product, angle) with an obtuse-angle clause; options available. About 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Component comparison of the cross product, then projection.
questions.justification: Chain of cross-product determinant, three linear equations, dot-product expansion and projection; routine but multi-step. Level 2 as 2026-P2-Q1.

questions.key_step: Triple product expansion, then one linear equation for alpha.
questions.justification: One recalled formula, one linear equation, one cross product magnitude; options for checking. Near 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), L1.

questions.key_step: Linear independence is the triple product being non-zero.
questions.justification: One familiar move: independence equals non-zero triple product, then a $3\times3$ determinant with a parameter that simplifies via a column operation. Options available. Close to 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) / 2021-P1-Q7 (L1), L1.

questions.key_step: Identity in x,y forces |a|^2=3|b|^2 and a.b=0.
questions.justification: Needs the idea that an identity in x,y splits into coefficient conditions, then Lagrange. Three short stages but standard; L2 like 2026-P2-Q1.

questions.key_step: Acute angle for every b>1 means u.v>0 for all t=ln b>0; t->0 gives -12<0.
questions.justification: One dot product, then a quadratic in t that must stay positive on t>0; the decisive observation (t->0+ gives -12) is short but easy to miss, options allow a check. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q3 (L2, routine chain) and slightly above the one-move 2024-P2-Q11 (L0).

questions.key_step: Expand a x (b x c) = (a.c)b - (a.b)c and compare coefficients of the non-parallel b and c.
questions.justification: A single familiar move (vector triple product expansion) followed by equating coefficients; two dot-product evaluations. Same one-formula flavour as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) but needs the independence argument for b and c, so L1.

questions.key_step: Use $\hat a\times\hat b\perp\hat a,\hat b$ with magnitude $\sin45^\circ$ to get three dot/norm values, then rationalise $164\cos^2\theta$.
questions.justification: Needs the orthogonality of the cross product, three separate dot products or norms, and then a surd-rationalisation finish where one slip changes the option; options help only at the end. Heavier chain than 2026-P2-Q1 (L3, similar vector-algebra evaluation).

questions.key_step: Four points coplanar iff [AB AC AD]=0; expand the 3x3 determinant and use product of roots.
questions.justification: One standard criterion (scalar triple product = 0) and a determinant expansion giving a quadratic; the product of roots comes from Vieta. Closest anchor 2023-P2-Q4 (L3, coplanarity checks of four position vectors) is richer, so this single-criterion item sits at L1.

questions.key_step: Coplanar vectors with equal angles must be at 120 deg; apply (a x b).(b x c) = (a.b)(b.c) - (a.c)(b.b) three times.
questions.justification: Deduce 120 deg, then three applications of the Lagrange-type identity and a symmetric simplification to 3/4 abc(a+b+c). Routine chain, no new idea beyond the identity; options available. Level matches 2026-P2-Q1 style chain but lighter.

questions.key_step: Both lines pass through (1,1,0), so the plane normal is d1 x d2 = (1+a)(1-a,1,1); distance condition gives a^2+2a-8=0.
questions.justification: Cross product with a parameter, plane equation, point-to-plane distance and a quadratic: four routine stages with no insight needed, but numerical format means no options to check. Nearest anchor 2026-P1-Q6 (L3, planes with distances) is multi-statement, so a notch lower.

questions.key_step: a x b = 4c etc. force a, b, c to be mutually perpendicular, so the magnitudes obey |a||b|=4|c|, |b||c|=9|a|, |c||a|=alpha|b|.
questions.justification: Recognising that each cross product being a multiple of the third vector makes the triple mutually perpendicular is a less drilled idea; then a magnitude system and one condition, with no options to check. Chain of three stages; closest anchor 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, vectors built from a,b,c) is harder, so L3.
Two standard identities applied once each; no decision beyond recognising them. One-trick level; numerical format only adds the lack of options. Similar demand to 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) with one more step.

questions.key_step: Normal of P is (line direction) x (normal of the other plane); then point-to-plane distance.
questions.justification: Two successive cross products (plane through two lines through the origin, then plane containing a line and perpendicular to a plane), plane equation and distance: routine multi-step with arithmetic risk, options help. Matches 2026-P1-Q6 style but with fewer statements, so L2.

questions.key_step: Normal of E = n1 x n2 = (-3,-3,0), so E: x+y=0; distance of Q(a,a,2) from E gives |a|=3.
questions.justification: Cross product of normals, plane through a point, point-to-plane distance and a squared distance: routine chain, no insight; options provide a check. Same demand as 2024-P1-Q16 (L3, plane distances) but shorter.

questions.key_step: Apply the skew-lines formula |(a1-a2).(b1 x b2)|/|b1 x b2| after reading both lines in standard form.
questions.justification: One standard formula; the only care is rewriting the second line (7-x)/2=y-2=z-6 as (x-7)/(-2)=(y-2)/1=(z-6)/1. Same single-formula demand as 2023-P1-Q5-type distance items but without any search, so L1.

questions.key_step: Direction of the required line is the cross product of the plane normals (1,1,-1) x (1,-2,3) = (1,-4,-3); then foot or |QP x b|/|b|.
questions.justification: Direction by cross product, then foot of perpendicular by a parameter and dot-product condition, then the length: three routine stages, options for checking. Slightly more than a single formula; no unfamiliar idea. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q7 (L4) in topic but much lighter.

questions.key_step: Perpendicularity of the planes fixes k=1; the plane through their intersection is a family member with x-intercept 1, fixing lambda=1/2.
questions.justification: Two stages: find k from perpendicular normals, then use the family-of-planes (P1 + lambda P2 = 0) with the x-intercept condition; intercept form read off at the end. Routine, options available. Level 2.

questions.key_step: Foot (2l-1,3l+3,1-l): perpendicularity gives a=7l-2, distance 2sqrt6 gives l=1 (a>0 rejects l=-3/5); image by midpoint.
questions.justification: Foot of perpendicular with two conditions (dot product and distance) leading to a quadratic, a sign check from a>0, then reflection by midpoint: a short chain with arithmetic care, options available. Level 2.

questions.key_step: Direction of the line of intersection is the cross product of the normals; sin of the angle with the plane fixes b = ±a.
questions.justification: Routine chain: cross product of normals, line-plane angle formula, then direction cosines. Options help, but the sign choice b = ±a is a trap (both signs satisfy the data). Like 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) in chain but shorter and fully standard.

questions.key_step: Foot of perpendicular as a linear map of $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, then invert and use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$.
questions.justification: Foot formula, two linear equations to solve for cos and sin, and elimination into a conic; each stage is standard but long, with arithmetic slips likely. Options allow checking by test points, so 3 not 4. Comparable to 2023-P2-Q4 (L3) in length.

questions.key_step: Coplanarity determinant gives $\lambda=3$; plane normal from the two direction vectors; test the points.
questions.justification: Standard chain: coplanarity determinant (3x3), cross product for the normal, plane equation, check four points. Nothing unfamiliar but several arithmetic stages; same demand as 2024-P1-Q16 (L3, direct) but with options to test, so 2.

questions.key_step: Normal as cross product of the two direction-ratio vectors; plane intercepts then tetrahedron volume $\frac16|\alpha\beta\gamma|$.
questions.justification: Four routine steps: normal, plane equation, intercepts, volume. No insight needed, options allow a check; matches 2026-P2-Q2 style chain (L2).

questions.key_step: Foot of perpendicular gives the normal direction $(2,1,3)$, so $m=1,n=3$; then intersect the slanted line with the plane.
questions.justification: Normal from the foot gives $m,n$ at once, then a single line-plane intersection. Routine; similar to 2026-P2-Q2 (L2).

questions.key_step: $\angle PRQ=60^\circ$ in the right triangle $PQR$ (right angle at $Q$) gives $QR=PQ\cot60^\circ$.
questions.justification: One familiar picture: distance of a point from a plane, then right-triangle trigonometry. Short and direct; at the same level as a single-formula JEE Main item, but three small calculations keep it above 0.

questions.key_step: Direction of the shortest-distance line is the cross product of directions; the angle condition (read with the normal) gives $a=2$; then reflect in the plane.
questions.justification: Three stages (cross product, angle condition to find $a$, reflection of a point) with no options. The printed condition is inconsistent, so careful reading is needed. Comparable to 2025-P1-Q5 (L4) in stages but each stage is standard.

questions.key_step: Points on the line at distance $\sqrt{26}$ from $P$ come from a quadratic in $\lambda$; area from the cross product.
questions.justification: Parametrise, solve a quadratic with integer roots, then a cross product and square: routine chain, 4 steps, no options so some slip risk. Like 2026-P2-Q1 (vector area) which was level 3 but with fewer stages here.

questions.key_step: The plane $3x-8y+7z=4$ contains $L$, so $\vec d_L\perp(3,-8,7)$ fixes $\ell=\frac23$; then the angle with the $y$-axis.
questions.justification: Reading the stem correctly, parameter $\ell$ from a perpendicularity condition, a cross product with parameter, then angle with an axis and a scaled answer; numerical with several algebraic stages. Level 3 as in 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, similar parameter hunt) but fewer ideas.

questions.key_step: Plane through a given line and a point of the pencil: use the pencil of planes through the second line, two conditions fix $a$ and $\lambda$.
questions.justification: Two unknowns ($a$ and the pencil parameter) fixed by one point and one perpendicularity condition, then the line-plane intersection; numerical with algebraic risk. Comparable to 2024-P1-Q12 (L4) but more routine.

questions.key_step: Diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular: $(\alpha,-1,\beta)\perp\overrightarrow{PQ}$; then the integer solution of minimum absolute values of a linear Diophantine equation.
questions.justification: Perpendicularity of diagonals gives $45\alpha+47\beta=30$; the real work is the Diophantine step with 'minimum absolute values' (check the other families of solutions). Level 3 for the number-theory twist; same style as 2024-P1-Q12 (L4) but shorter.

questions.key_step: Two perpendicularity conditions give $a=2b$ and $b^2=1$; then substitute the line point into the plane.
questions.justification: Two dot-product equations, a small substitution, then a line-plane intersection; each step routine. Level 2 by chain length (comparable to 2026-P2-Q3, L2).
